The incubation biology of the Glossy black cockatoo (Calyptorhynchus lathami) reveals several critical life-history constraints. Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] require a developmental period of 30 days [ab = 30 days] to reach hatching, a duration that aligns with the prolonged embryonic development observed in other Australian cockatoo species. The newly hatched nestling emerges with a wet weight of 22 grams [Wwb = 22 grams], reflecting the substantial metabolic costs incurred during organogenesis and albumen buffering within the calcareous shell. This neonatal mass is a critical starting point for the subsequent growth trajectory of the altricial nestling, which is entirely dependent on biparental provisioning during its early development within the nest hollow.

The nestling period is marked by an extreme acceleration in mass gain as the developing chick transitions from yolk-dependent embryo to an actively fed, feather-growing nestling. Under the core body temperatures typical of active metabolic function in this species (41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]), the fledgling precursor reaches a critical milestone: the time since birth at fledging is 90 days [tx = 90 days], a protracted period that reflects the slow, K-selected life-history strategy of this bird. By this point, the nestling has achieved a substantial portion of its asymptotic growth. The ultimate wet weight attained by the nestling is 520 grams [Wwi = 520 grams], a figure that slightly exceeds the typical adult weight of approximately 450 grams, as nestlings often accumulate fat reserves as an energetic buffer before the energetically demanding transition to nutritional independence.

The maturation timeline of the Glossy black cockatoo is exceptionally long, even by psittaciform standards. Sexual maturation, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and the first surge of reproductive hormones, does not occur until the time since birth at puberty of 270 days [tp = 270 days] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. However, this physiological readiness does not translate immediately into breeding activity. Under the consistent thermal conditions of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], which is optimal for peak physiological performance in this species, the first reproduction event is significantly delayed. The time since birth at first brood is 3 years [tR = 3 years], a latency that is likely driven by the need to secure a permanent nest hollow—a fiercely contested and limited resource in sclerophyll forests—and to establish a stable pair bond before committing to the high energetic demands of egg production and chick rearing at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C].

Longevity data underscore the species' position at the slow end of the life-history continuum. Field records and captive colony data indicate that the maximum lifespan is approximately 37.7 years [am = approximately 37.7 years], making it one of the longest-lived cockatoo species relative to at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C] its body size. This remarkable longevity is believed to be linked to a low extrinsic mortality rate, facilitated by strong flight capabilities, a generalist diet of casuarina cones, and the safety provided by roosting and nesting in elevated tree hollows. This extended lifespan is evolutionarily coupled with a consistently low annual reproductive output. Under the thermally optimal conditions of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is constrained by both clutch size and breeding frequency.

The species exhibits a highly conservative reproductive strategy. Females typically lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], which is a common trait among large cockatoos that invest heavily in each offspring. Furthermore, a single clutch is produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch is produced each year], and this annual breeding attempt is often only successful if the preceding wet season has provided sufficient food resources for the female to achieve the necessary body condition. This low annual fecundity, combined with the long delays before first reproduction and the high juvenile mortality associated with predation and competition for nest sites, results in a population turnover rate that is exceptionally slow. The species is thus highly vulnerable to habitat loss, particularly the removal of old-growth trees that provide the large hollows essential for nesting, as the population cannot quickly compensate for increased adult mortality through elevated recruitment.
